I'd like to add a few points about Venture Capital in particular, which wasn't mentioned enough:

  1. Mandatory exit. Venture capitalists are in it just for the money. VC will set a time frame and will cash out at the end of that term. For Reddit that was 10 years. You didn't think all this was just coincidence with their 10th anniversary did you?

  2. Loss of independence You may still be the chief executive officer, but you answer to the board now and it's not just your company anymore. The VCs will ask for one or more board seats and the right to veto key decisions and control the firm's capital structure.

  3. They will have the right to fire you and your management team. You could find yourself reporting to a new CEO, or be ousted from the company you founded

  4. Anti-dilution protection. If the company's stock price goes down any time in the future, they get additional stock for free.

  5. Dividends. In addition to stock, they get a guaranteed rate of return.

  6. Liquidation preferences. VCs get their principal and dividends back before anyone else gets a penny.

  7. Participating preferred. They get to double dip—they first get their investment plus dividends, then the value of their stock.

  8. Mandatory redemption. This requires the company to buy their stock back by a certain date, establishing a deadline for an exit event.

  9. Demand registration rights. The VCs can force the company to file a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission to initiate an initial public offering—another way of forcing an exit event. Reddit is not big enough for this to be worthwhile.

  10. Approval rights. The VCs must approve any new financings and have the right to participate.

  11. Reps and warranties. You'll also have to accept personal liability for representations you've made about key aspects of the company. They will have the right to sue you for all you own if you forgot to give them any bad news.

[source]

Hey everyone, I work at an MSP, and we've been discussing the merits of Hyper-V Shared Nothing vs. traditional HA SAN clusters in small to medium sized businesses.

Other than the obviously reduced cost of Shared Nothing and the not quite instant failover, do you all have any opinions or experience on this topic? What are the common mistakes and gotchas that may not be apparent at first glance?
Advice on Hyper-V Shared Nothing setups

The only time that "shared nothing" comes into play is the conversation of VM migration to another host. It's not a setup or configuration, it's a method of migration. It's an option, yes, but it's far from preferred. There's no "merits" to this situation other than cost, but you're not losing nothing with that savings--there's a ton to lose. If any part goes down migration is impossible.

From what I've read comparing shared nothing vs SAN HA is comparing Apples to Oranges. In most cases a small or medium business should always use local storage for their VMs, unless they have 3 hosts give or take. If an environment requires a SAN because downtime is not an option and the amount of money that will be lost is great, having redundant SANS with HA turned on is a must.
I finally setup my first Hyper-V Failover Cluster and I am extremely happy, I was able to pull down the whole system for under 50k with 3 cluster nodes and redundant shared storage.

In server 2016, there's the new option of shared nothing failover cluster. It doesn't scale and it's meant for small setups but with 4 servers with local storage you can make a storage cluster. You're wasting lots of space though.

At work we have a storagespaces cluster connected to hyper-v compute nodes with infiniband and it is scary fast. One of my happiest days in IT was telling EMC to gtfo and never come back. We now have 21TB of storage for less than 10k. I got a raise for it.

This is more what I was looking for. I realize that there'd be a lot of wasted space, but even with all that wasted space, it's still going to be cheaper than going EqualLogic or XIO. I'll check out a setup similar to yours and see if it's what the PM is looking for. Thank you!

My full set up is as follows:

2x small servers each with a 2 port Infiniband card, 2 port SAS card, 32 GB ram running Server 2012 R2 in a Failover Cluster.

1x 24 bay SAS cabinet from DataOn (http://www.dataonstorage.com/dataon-solutions/windows-server-2012-storage-spaces-solutions.html) w/12 near line SAS 1.8TB 7200 RPM drives, 8 15000 RPM drives, and just adding 4 STeC 200GB SSDS

2x Mellanox 4036 36 port 32Gbs Infiniband switches

The rest is gb ethernet for now. The storage is expressed as SMB shares via this cluster to the rest of the enterprise to be consumed as needed. Everything is so low latency that the SAS controller is now the bottleneck. You can run Hyper-V, SQL Server DBs, VDI VHDXs, etc from SMB3 share and because I'm using the Infinband, I get RDMA (or SMBDirect) and it all flows from the NICs and there's not CPU involvement. I usually see latencies the same as if I was directly attached to the drives. It's like the network isn't even there.
